## What the skill does

The `landslide-pipelines` skill (`.claude/skills/landslide-pipelines/SKILL.md` in this repo)
lets Claude Code run the whole landslide-mapping method for one study area and write up the
results:

| Step | Script | Produces |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Align and its inputs | `R/run_align_pipeline.R` → `R/align_supervisor.R` | aligned DTM, DoD, outlier and exceedance rasters, level of detection, gradient raster, `align_run\*.csv` |
| 2. RIL (runs alongside 1) | `R/ril_pipeline.R` | landform raster |
| 3. LShunter and LSstats | `R/lshunter_lsstats_pipeline.R` | candidate-landslide patch raster, patch table (volumes ± SD), LSstats csv files, and the patches as a polygon shapefile; with `lshunter_deposits: TRUE`, the deposits below each scar (raster, table, polygons) and each scar's volume balance |
| 4. Strip noise (optional, off by default; runs alongside 3) | `R/strip_noise.R`, as Stage 4 of `R/run_align_pipeline.R` | each survey's noise between its own flight passes: strip offsets and a noise floor by canopy, slope and ground density |
| Report | `PipelineReport.qmd` | one self-contained html file |
| Review (optional, afterwards) | `R/scar_review.R`, `R/naip_images.R` | a labelling page for a stratified sample of the candidates, with lidar panels and optional NAIP aerial photos |

Step 4 is a diagnostic of the surveys, not an input to the results, and runs only with
`noise_run: TRUE` in the site file. It measures each survey's noise where two of its flight passes
overlap (no real change between passes flown minutes apart). The report then shows the offsets
between passes -- above about 0.1 m is a systematic strip error, which appears in the change map
along flight lines -- and the pass noise as a floor under Align's level of detection. It adds
about 40 minutes of computing per survey (Site 1), which is why it is off unless asked for.

Every input for a site goes in **one site file** of `keyword: value` lines (template
`R/site_template.txt`). `R/run_site.R` reads it, writes each pipeline's configuration file, and
runs the driver `R/run_landslide_pipelines.R`, which runs the steps in order and renders the
report. Claude fills in the site file, starts the run, follows its progress, writes the
interpretation from the outputs, and renders the report.

## The site file

Keywords are grouped by prefix: `site_` (names, folders, polygon, CRS), `ref_` and `align_` for
the two surveys (label, LAZ, DTM and DSM), `ground_` (ground-return counts), `align_` (Align
settings), `ril_` (the RIL chain's three Fortran input files), `lshunter_`, `lsstats_` and
`noise_` (strip noise, off unless `noise_run: TRUE`), and `naip_` (NAIP photos of every patch;
off unless `naip_run: TRUE`).
Anything left out takes its default, and an unknown keyword stops the run. Everything that links
one program to the next is filled in: Align's output names come from the run folder and the
survey labels; LShunter reads Align's exceedance raster, gradient, centred difference, IQR raster
and noise correlogram, and RIL's landform raster; LSstats reads LShunter's patch raster and patch
table. In `lsstats_rasters`, `@cendif`, `@exceed`, `@dif`, `@outlier`, `@lod`, `@gradient` and
`@aligned` stand for this run's Align outputs. For Site 2 the file is
`C:\Work\Data\Site2\Site2_2017_2025.txt` (Site 1: `C:\Work\Data\Site1\Site1_2017_2023.txt`).

```
Rscript R/run_site.R C:\Work\Data\Site2\Site2_2017_2025.txt --configs-only   # check only
Rscript R/run_site.R C:\Work\Data\Site2\Site2_2017_2025.txt                  # run everything
```

Outputs go to `<site_dir>\<site_run_name>\`, the generated configurations to its `configs\`
folder. The configurations are rewritten on every run, so change settings in the site file. Give
each survey its DTM and DSM tile folders (`ref_dtm_tile_dir`, `ref_dsm_tile_dir`, ...) and put the
mosaics (`ref_dtm`, `ref_dsm`, ...) in the run folder, so that a new run builds its own; the
ground-return counts go in each survey's `ground_dir` (e.g. `<survey>\grnd_den`) and are reused by
later runs on the same reference DTM.

**Water and gaps in coverage** are left out of Align, and so out of the change maps and the
candidates, by default:

- lakes, from `site_water_polygons` (with `site_water_layer` and `site_water_where`, e.g.
  `FCode = 39000`, for a geodatabase). Lakes only: rivers move between surveys, so they come from
- the surveys' own water returns (LAS class 9, counted beside the ground returns), and flat open
  water;
- coverage gaps: 50 m blocks where either survey has fewer than 0.02 ground returns per m²
  (missing or snow-covered tiles; `align_coverage: FALSE` keeps them).

Align writes `watermask_<tag>` in the run folder, saying why each cell was left out (1 water
polygon, 2 water returns, 3 flat water, 4 no coverage; `align_outWaterMask: FALSE` turns it off).
A 50 m block straddling the edge of a missing tile can still pass the coverage rule, so a strip of
up to 50 m along such an edge stays in.

A site file holds full paths: the data, the RIL input files (which name their own DEM, scratch
and output paths) and the executable folders (`align_executable_dir`,
`ril_bldgrds_executable_dir`, `ril_valleyfloor_executable_dir`, `ril_executable_dir`,
`lshunter_executable_dir`, `lsstats_executable_dir`). On another computer, copy the site file and
the RIL input files and change every path that differs there; `--configs-only` stops on any input
or executable it can't find.

## One-time setup on each computer

1. **Clone or pull the repos** into one `repos` folder, on these branches:

   | Repo | Branch | Holds |
   |---|---|---|
   | UnstableSlopes (`DanMillerM2`) | `main` | the R scripts, the skill, this guide |
   | TWutils (`DanMillerM2`) | `main` (c2290a4 or later) | the R package that writes the programs' input files |
   | GridUtilities (`teal-waters`) | `master` (ab662ea or later) | Align, bldgrds |
   | LandslideUtilities (`DanMillerM2`) | `master` (tag `lshunter-1.4.0` or later) | LShunter, LSstats |
   | ChannelUtilities (`teal-waters`) | `master` | ValleyFloor, RIL |
   | modules (`teal-waters`) | `master` | Fortran modules shared by all of the above |

2. **Copy the Visual Studio projects.** The project files (`.sln`, `.vfproj`) are not in the
   repos: each program is built by a project under `<Repo>\Projects\<Name>\`, a folder beside
   `repos` (for example `C:\Work\Sandbox\GridUtilities\Projects\align` next to
   `C:\Work\Sandbox\repos\GridUtilities`). The projects find their source by relative path
   (`..\..\..\repos\GridUtilities\...`), so copy the `GridUtilities`, `LandslideUtilities` and
   `ChannelUtilities` project folders from a computer that has them, keeping that layout. Two
   exceptions: LSstats's project is `LandslideUtilities\LSstats\` (not under `Projects\`), and
   RIL's project includes Intel MKL's `lapack.f90` from
   `C:\Program Files (x86)\IntelSWTools\compilers_and_libraries_2020.4.311\...`, so on a computer
   with another Intel Fortran version, point that file at its MKL.
3. **Build the executables** in Visual Studio, Release|x64: `align` (GridUtilities 8a08fa6 or
   later; ab662ea or later for the optional `align_exceedanceTrim`, 78b4911 for
   `align_suspectGround`, 2083edb for `align_matchSmoothness`; Align 1.1.0, tag `align-1.1.0`, for
   the water and coverage masks), `bldgrds`, `ValleyFloor`, `RIL`, `LShunter` (1.1.0 or later;
   1.4.0 for deposits) and `LSstats` (1.1.0 or later). Build from the pulled source, so each
   executable matches a commit; an executable older than its source is the first thing to suspect
   when a run behaves unexpectedly.
4. **Install the R packages**: TWutils (`R CMD INSTALL TWutils` from the `repos` folder, on
   `main`), plus `terra`, `sf`, `lasR`, `lidR`, `future`, `future.apply`, `processx`, `ggplot2`,
   `knitr` and `jsonlite`. An older TWutils stops Align at the start with "The installed TWutils is older
   than this pipeline", naming what's missing.
5. **Put Quarto on the PATH**, so that `quarto --version` works in a new terminal. RStudio has a
   copy that isn't on the PATH (`C:\Program Files\RStudio\resources\app\bin\quarto\bin`); either
   add that folder to the PATH or install Quarto from <https://quarto.org>.
6. **Copy `PipelineReport.qmd`** into the UnstableSlopes folder from a computer that has it. The
   report template is kept out of git because it is adapted to each study site. Without it,
   Claude writes a new one from the skill's description and shows it to you first.

The skill checks the R packages, TWutils and Quarto before it starts and says what is missing; an
executable that is too old is caught a few seconds after it starts.

## Running a site

Start Claude Code in this repo, so that the skill is loaded:

```
cd C:\Work\Sandbox\Repos\unstableslopes
claude
```

Then type `/landslide-pipelines`, or ask in your own words. With a site file:

> Run the landslide pipelines for `C:\Work\Data\Site2\Site2_2017_2025.txt`.

Or without one:

> Run the landslide pipelines for Site 3, 2018 to 2024. Site folder `C:\Work\Data\Site3`,
> study area `C:\Work\Data\Site3\study_area.shp`. Use the Site 2 site file and RIL inputs as
> templates.

Without a site file, Claude asks, in one message, for anything it still needs:

- study name, output folder, study-area polygon and target CRS (default EPSG:2856);
- for each survey (older reference, newer to align): DTM tiles or file, LAZ tiles, and DSM tiles
  or file. All three are required: the LAZ tiles give the density-based level of detection, the
  exceedance raster, the water returns and coverage gaps (and the strip noise, if run), and Align
  uses both DSMs for canopy height;
- a lake polygon layer, if there is one;
- the complete DTM for RIL, and the bldgrds, ValleyFloor and RIL input files to copy;
- LShunter and LSstats settings (thresholds, flow-accumulation raster, rasters to summarize);
- executable folders, if they aren't the defaults.

## What happens next

1. **Checks.** Claude runs the prerequisite checks. The report template, `PipelineReport.qmd`, is
   tracked in git, so every checkout renders the same report format; if it is missing, Claude
   restores it from git.
2. **Site file.** It writes (or checks) the site file and runs `run_site.R --configs-only`. Align
   uses its defaults unless the file says otherwise: tiles chosen by cross-validation, iterations
   stopping once the aligned DEM changes by less than 5 mm, central derivatives and the
   density-based level of detection. Claude shows you the site file, the Align settings and
   LShunter's inputs and thresholds before running.
3. **Run.** The driver runs in the background. A rebuild from tiles takes a few hours: at Site 1
   (390 million cells) the ground-return counts took about 35 minutes for the two surveys, Align
   39 minutes, LShunter with deposits 21 and LSstats 7. Run one site's Align at a time: Align
   holds whole DEMs in memory (about 48 GB). Claude reports each Align milestone (global fit
   converged, tiles chosen, tile loop converged) and stops with the cause if a step fails. After
   Align, LShunter and LSstats run (beside the strip noise, if it is on). Don't edit the R
   scripts while a run is using them: R reads a script as it runs, so an edit can break the
   running copy.
4. **Interpretation.** Claude reads the run's tables and writes `<report_dir>\narrative.md`: the
   tiles chosen and how clear the choice was, convergence, RMSE and the level of detection, the
   pattern of shifts, the candidate landslides with volumes ± SD against the sign-flip control,
   their landforms, the deposits, how much was left out as water or for missing coverage, (with
   strip noise) the strip offsets and how much of the noise each survey explains on its own, and
   caveats. Every number comes from the output files.
5. **Report.** `run_site.R` is rerun; it skips every finished step and renders
   `<report_dir>\<study_name>_report.html`. The file is self-contained and can be emailed as is.

## The patch polygons

After LSstats, `R/patch_polygons.R` writes the candidate landslides as a polygon shapefile,
`<run folder>\patch_<ref>_<align>_polygons.shp`, one feature per patch, for use in a GIS. With
deposits on (see Deposits below), the deposits are features of the same shapefile: the field
`type` is `scar` or `deposit`, and a deposit's `scar` field holds the label of the scar it came
from, so selecting a scar and its deposits is one query. Its attribute table holds everything
known about each patch:

- from LShunter's patch table: cells and area, centroid, mean and deepest elevation change,
  volume with its SD and z, mean and maximum gradient, the most extreme S, shares of valley floor,
  hollow and inner gorge, distance to channel, false-discovery rates from the null simulation and
  the sign-flip control, and (when computed) canopy height in both surveys;
- from the polygon: perimeter, and the length and width of its minimum rotated rectangle;
- from LSstats: the landform it lies in, distance to the floodplain edge, and the minimum, median
  and maximum of each raster LSstats summarized (`lsstats_rasters`).

Shapefile field names are limited to 10 characters, so `<...>_polygons_fields.csv` beside it
gives each field's source, units and meaning. Missing values (-9999) are null. The shapefile is
rewritten whenever the patch raster, patch table or LSstats files are newer.

## Deposits

With `lshunter_deposits: TRUE` in the site file (LShunter 1.4.0 or later), LShunter also looks
for the material each scar delivered downslope:

- **Runout paths.** From every scar, flow is traced down the reference (older) DTM's flow
  directions, which bldgrds computes once into `ang_<ref>` in the run folder. Distance along a
  path counts from the last point of coherent loss -- the scar itself, or scour along a
  debris-flow track -- so a long scoured track doesn't use up the allowance; a path ends
  `lshunter_dep_max_distance` (500 m) beyond it, or where it enters another scar.
- **Corridors.** Everything within `lshunter_dep_spread` (100 m) of a path, saved as
  `corridor_<tag>` (each cell holds the scar it belongs to).
- **Deposits.** Patches of significant gain (S of 4 to seed, 2 to grow, the reverse of the scars'
  thresholds). Seeds must lie out of channels and off the valley floor; a deposit may then extend
  into a narrow channel or onto the floodplain, but only where that is contiguous with gain
  outside it. A gain patch is a deposit of the scar whose corridor holds most of its seed cells
  (and only cells no higher than their path). Gain patches with no scar above them are kept
  separately, as "unlinked": a check on the gain-side level of detection, and a list of gains
  (fill, vegetation read as ground, slow deep-seated movement) worth a look.

Outputs: `patch_<tag>_deposits` and `_unlinked` rasters, `patch_<tag>_table_deposits.csv` (every
patch-table column, plus the scar, travel distance, drop, reach angle, and channel share),
`_unlinked.csv`, `_balance.csv` (each scar's volume against its deposits', the net and their SDs
from the correlated noise, and the deposit/scar ratio, near 1 to 1.3 where little left the
slope); the deposits are also in `patch_<tag>_polygons.shp` (see below). With `lshunter_null_realizations`, each deposit's
false-discovery rate comes from simulated noise patches that land in the same corridors.

## Reviewing the candidates

LShunter's patches are candidates: some are landslide scars, others are real change of another
kind (harvest, roads, channel erosion) or artifacts (vegetation classified as ground, gaps in
ground returns, misalignment). `R/scar_review.R` builds a web page for judging a sample of them by
eye. Its labels give the share of candidates that are scars, and are the ground truth for finding
which patch attributes separate scars from the rest.

### What the page shows

One candidate at a time, in shuffled order:

- **Eight lidar panels**: both surveys' hillshades (the newer one after Align), the elevation
  change from -1 to +1 m, a 700 m context hillshade, both surveys' canopy height, and both surveys'
  ground returns per m². The candidate is outlined in magenta, other candidates in dashed yellow.
  On the ground-return panels, what Align leaves out is masked: each survey's coverage gaps
  (missing tiles) in grey, and water in blue, so that no returns there isn't read as thin ground
  cover. The patch statistics give each candidate's share in a gap and in water.
- **NAIP aerial photos** (optional): for each NAIP year, a close-up and a 350 m view, with the
  flight date in each title. NAIP is flown with leaves on at 0.6-1 m, so it shows the canopy, not
  the ground under it. It helps most where the canopy opened or was never closed: harvest units,
  roads, fresh bare soil, debris tracks. Change after the latest flight doesn't show; Washington's
  latest NAIP is 2023, so a 2025 survey is compared with 2023 photos.
- **A verdict**: landslide scar, other real change, artifact, or can't tell (keys 1-4). For a
  scar, how well the outline fits (matches, too large, too small, part of a bigger scar, several
  merged, includes the deposit). For other change or an artifact, why (vegetation as ground,
  ground-return gap, canopy change, misalignment, DTM seam, water, road, channel, logging, tree
  throw, deposit, other). A note box for anything else.
- **Patch statistics**, hidden until opened (key S) so they don't steer the verdict, with a link
  to a satellite view.

Each reviewer's labels are kept separately, so several people can review the same sample; the
queue at the bottom shows how many others have labelled each candidate.

### The sample

The sample is stratified, so that rare kinds of candidate are seen often enough to judge. Only scars are
sampled: with deposits on, the patch shapefile also holds the deposits, which the page leaves out
(as does `R/naip_images.R`). Each
patch goes into one level of each **factor**; the strata are the combinations of levels, and
`per_stratum` patches are drawn at random from each (all of them where there are fewer). A factor
is a line of `level = condition` pairs, in terms of the patch shapefile's fields (listed in
`<...>_polygons_fields.csv`). The first true condition wins, `otherwise` takes the rest, and a
missing value counts as false. Without any factor lines the sample uses these two, six strata in
all:

```
factor_fdr: sig = sim_fdr <= 0.05; nonsig = otherwise
factor_canopy: loss = canopy_chg < -10; growth = canopy_chg > 5; mid = otherwise
```

That is, null-simulation false-discovery rate at most 5% or not, crossed with canopy height
falling by more than 10 m, growing by more than 5 m, or neither. `sim_fdr` exists only when the
run used the null simulation (`lshunter_null_realizations`); without it, stratify on the
sign-flip control's rate instead (`factor_fdr: sig = flip_fdr <= 0.05; nonsig = otherwise`), as
the Site 1 and Site 2 rebuilds of November 2026 do. A `filter` line restricts the
sample to patches meeting a condition (for example `filter: area_m2 >= 50`). The same shapefile,
factors and seed always give the same sample, so a page rebuilt later keeps its labels.

### Building and publishing the page

1. Copy `R/scar_review_params_template.txt` and set at least the run folder and an output folder:

   ```
   run_dir: C:\Work\Data\Site2\run_17_25
   out_dir: C:\Work\Data\Site2\run_17_25\scar_review
   title: Site 2 scar review
   per_stratum: 40
   naip: TRUE
   ```

   Everything else is found from the run folder's configuration files: the patch shapefile and
   raster, the elevation change, both surveys' DTMs, DSMs, ground- and water-return counts,
   Align's water mask, the aligned DTM and the survey years. Each can also be given directly (see
   the template).

2. Run it:

   ```
   Rscript R/scar_review.R C:\Work\Data\Site2\scar_review_params_site2.txt
   ```

   The lidar panels take one to two seconds per patch, and are redrawn when the shapefile or
   `scar_review.R` is newer. NAIP photos are read over the network from
   Microsoft Planetary Computer (no account needed), 5-10 seconds per patch per worker, so 240
   patches take 10-20 minutes. Finished images are kept on a rerun, and a patch whose photos
   failed to download gets none; rerunning retries it, and meanwhile the page simply leaves the
   NAIP row out for that patch. With `naip: FALSE` (the default) the page has no NAIP row.

3. Ask Claude to publish it:

   > Publish the scar review in `C:\Work\Data\Site2\run_17_25\scar_review`.

   The page saves labels only as a private claude.ai page that keeps a database of what reviewers
   enter; opened from disk (`index.html`, which holds the sample) it shows every candidate but
   can't save. A new sample (after a rerun) has new candidates, so publish it as a new page, or
   accept that labels on the old page no longer match. Claude publishes it and gives you
   the link. It is private until you share it from the page's Share menu; each reviewer needs a
   claude.ai account and edit access to save labels.

### Using the labels

Ask Claude to read the labels, for example:

> Read the Site 2 scar review labels and estimate the share of candidates that are scars.

Because the strata were sampled at different rates, each stratum's verdicts are weighted by its
number of patches in the whole run (`population` in `patches.json`) to estimate rates for all
candidates. The labels can then be compared with patch attributes -- canopy change, ground-return
coverage in each survey, landform, size and shape, false-discovery rates -- to find thresholds
that would drop artifacts without losing scars.

### NAIP photos for every patch

`R/naip_images.R` also runs on its own, for any patches in a patch shapefile (template
`R/naip_images_params_template.txt`; `labels: ALL` or a list), writing `p<label>_naip.jpg` into
any folder. In a site file, `naip_run: TRUE` makes the pipeline run it for every candidate after
the patch polygons, into `<run folder>\naip\`. That takes hours for a large site, so it is off by
default; a failure there is reported but doesn't stop the run.

## Afterwards

- **Edit the wording**: change `narrative.md` yourself, or ask Claude to revise it, then ask for
  a re-render.
- **Change a parameter**: edit the site file. Claude asks before deleting the outputs the change
  affects, then reruns;
  only the missing outputs are rebuilt.
- **Resume after a failure**: ask Claude to run it again. Every step skips the outputs it already
  has.
- **Rerun one program by hand**: each script also runs on its own, for example
  `Rscript R/align_supervisor.R params.txt`; see the header of each script.
